# Setting

<!-- Section budget: 5 minutes, 5 slides. -->

## Election audits: when and why

- An election reports an outcome. A *risk-limiting audit* checks it against the paper ballots [@stark2008rla; @agitrla].
- If the reported outcome is wrong, the audit escalates to a full hand count with probability at least $1-\alpha$.
- If it is right, we would like to confirm that from as few ballots as possible.
- Used in practice: TODO add the jurisdictions you want to name (US states, pilot audits), with sources.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The when: after the count, before certification.
The why: paper ballots are the ground truth, and the audit is the only step that looks at them statistically.
:::

## Ballot polling is a sequential test

- Draw ballots uniformly at random, one at a time: $X_1, X_2, \dots$
- After each draw, either stop and certify, or keep sampling.
- $H_0$: the reported winner did not win. Certifying is rejecting $H_0$.
- *Risk-limiting* means level $\alpha$ under the audit's stopping rule, whatever it is:
$$\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta_0} P_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\text{certify}) \le \alpha.$$
- Throughout: sampling with replacement, so the $X_t$ are i.i.d.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
Flag with-replacement early; the backup slide has the finite-population argument if asked.
:::

## Two candidates: a Bernoulli test

- $\theta$ is the reported winner's share, $X_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta)$.
- $H_0: \theta \le 1/2$ against $H_1: \theta > 1/2$.
- BRAVO [@bravo2012] and ALPHA [@alpha_mart] solve this well.

```{.tikz width="75%"}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=12cm, y=1cm]
  % Null H0: theta <= 1/2, shaded as in the ternary diagrams
  \fill[black!12] (0,0) rectangle (0.5,1.4);

  % Axis
  \draw[thick] (0,0) -- (1,0);
  \foreach \x/\l in {0/0, 1/1} \draw (\x,0.12) -- (\x,-0.12) node[below] {$\l$};
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (0.5,0.2) -- (0.5,-0.2) node[below] {$1/2$ (tie)};
  \node[right] at (1.02,0) {$\theta$};

  % Region labels
  \node at (0.25,0.7) {$H_0$};
  \node at (0.75,0.7) {$H_1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
Keep this short. The point to plant is that the null is an interval with one boundary point, the tie.
:::

## Reading a ternary diagram

```{=html}

<script>GW.reader({ fig: "gw-reader", point: [0.45, 0.35, 0.20] });</script>
```

::: notes
Timing: 1.5 minutes. This slide carries the rest of the talk, so do not rush it.
Three candidates: theta = (theta1, theta2, theta3) with theta1 + theta2 + theta3 = 1.
Each vertex is a unanimous election; the centre is the three-way tie.
Distance from the edge opposite a vertex is that candidate's share.
Move the cursor around: to a vertex, the centre, the two-way ties at the midpoints of the left and right edges.
Take the cursor off the diagram and the pointer returns to the example election (0.45, 0.35, 0.20),
the alternative used in every widget; read its three coordinates aloud.
:::

## Three candidates: the plurality null

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $\Theta_1 = \{\theta_1 > \theta_2 \text{ and } \theta_1 > \theta_3\}$
- $\Theta_0 = \{\theta_1 \le \theta_2\} \cup \{\theta_1 \le \theta_3\}$
- A union of two half-spaces, and not convex.
- Its convex hull is $\{\theta_1 \le 1/2\}$.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.tikz width="100%"}
\usetikzlibrary{calc}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  % Simplex vertices: \theta_1 (top), theta_2 (bottom-left), theta_3 (bottom-right)
  \coordinate (T1) at (4,6.928);
  \coordinate (T2) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (T3) at (8,0);

  % Barycentric helper points
  \coordinate (G)   at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1,T3=1); % centroid (1/3,1/3,1/3)
  \coordinate (M12) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1);      % midpoint of T1--T2 edge
  \coordinate (M13) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T3=1);      % midpoint of T1--T3 edge

  % Shade H1 region: candidate 1 is the plurality winner
  \fill[black!12] (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Simplex outline
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Decision boundaries theta1=theta2 and theta1=theta3
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M12) -- (G);
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (G)   -- (M13);

  % Region labels
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.5,T2=0.25,T3=0.25) {$H_1$};
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.2,T2=0.4,T3=0.4)   {$H_0$};

  % Boundary labels
  \node[font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.35,T2=0.5,T3=0.15) {$\theta_1=\theta_2$};
  \node[font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.35,T2=0.15,T3=0.5) {$\theta_1=\theta_3$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
  \node[below right] at (T3) {$\theta_3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The non-convexity is the source of every difficulty that follows; say it in those words.
The gap between the null and its hull is where candidate 1 has a plurality but not a majority.
:::

# The question

<!-- Section budget: 2 minutes, 2 slides. -->

## The state of the art runs one test per pair

::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 50%; text-align: center;"}
```{.tikz height="400px"}

\begin{tikzpicture}

  \coordinate (M12) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1);  % midpoint of T1--T2 edge

  % Shade H_1^{(2)} region: theta1 > theta2  (T1 side of the M12--T3 line)
  \fill[black!12] (T2) -- (T3) -- (M12) -- cycle;

  % Simplex outline
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Boundary theta1 = theta2
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M12) -- (T3);

  % Region labels

  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.2,T2=0.5,T3=0.3) {$H_0^{(2)}$};

  % Boundary label
  \node[font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.35,T2=0.5,T3=0.15) {$\theta_1=\theta_2$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
  \node[below right] at (T3) {$\theta_3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
:::
::: {.column style="width: 50%; text-align: center;"}
```{.tikz height="400px"}
\usetikzlibrary{calc}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \coordinate (T1) at (4,6.928);
  \coordinate (T2) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (T3) at (8,0);
  \coordinate (M13) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T3=1);  % midpoint of T1--T3 edge

  % Shade H_1^{(3)} region: theta1 > theta3  (T1 side of the M13--T2 line)
  \fill[black!12] (T3) -- (T2) -- (M13) -- cycle;

  % Simplex outline
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % Boundary theta1 = theta3
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M13) -- (T2);

  % Region labels
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.5,T2=0.3,T3=0.2) {$H_1^{(3)}$};
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.2,T2=0.3,T3=0.5) {$H_0^{(3)}$};

  % Boundary label
  \node[font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.35,T2=0.15,T3=0.5) {$\theta_1=\theta_3$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
  \node[below right] at (T3) {$\theta_3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
:::
:::

- SHANGRLA [@stark2020shangrla]: test $H_{02}: \theta_1 \le \theta_2$ and $H_{03}: \theta_1 \le \theta_3$ separately, each at level $\alpha$.
- Certify when every pairwise null is rejected: an intersection-union test [@Berger1982].

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
Valid and convenient, since each pair is a one-dimensional problem we already know how to solve.
:::

## Why not just do one test? {.center}

::: {.bigq}
Two tests are valid.<br>
Is one test on the original null better?
:::

- At a fixed sample size, intersection-union tests can be inadmissible [@Berger1994].
- For sequential tests, measured in ballots sampled, nobody knows.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
This is the thesis question. Say it as "what does the decomposition cost, in ballots?"
:::

# Why it is hard

<!-- Section budget: 2 minutes, 2 slides. -->

## Bayesian tests handle the null directly

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Put a prior $W_1$ on $\Theta_1$ and $W_0$ on $\Theta_0$.
- Bayes factor $B_t = p_{W_1}(X^t) / p_{W_0}(X^t)$ needs no decomposition.
- Bayesian audits do this [@bayesian_audits; @Huang_2020].
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{.tikz width="100%"}
\usetikzlibrary{calc}
\definecolor{wone}{HTML}{0072B2}   % Okabe-Ito blue       -> W_1
\definecolor{wzero}{HTML}{D55E00}  % Okabe-Ito vermillion -> W_0
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \coordinate (T1) at (4,6.928);
  \coordinate (T2) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (T3) at (8,0);
  \coordinate (G)   at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1,T3=1);
  \coordinate (M12) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T2=1);
  \coordinate (M13) at (barycentric cs:T1=1,T3=1);

  % H0 shading (bottom region)
  \fill[black!8] (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;

  % W1 contours (prior under the alternative), clipped to H1
  \begin{scope}
    \clip (T1) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- cycle;
    \input{contours_h1.tex}
  \end{scope}

  % W0 contours (prior under the null), clipped to H0
  \begin{scope}
    \clip (T2) -- (M12) -- (G) -- (M13) -- (T3) -- cycle;
    \input{contours_h0.tex}
  \end{scope}

  % Simplex outline + decision boundaries
  \draw[thick] (T1) -- (T2) -- (T3) -- cycle;
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (M12) -- (G);
  \draw[line width=1.1pt] (G)   -- (M13);

  % Region + prior labels
  \node at (barycentric cs:T1=0.62,T2=0.19,T3=0.19) {$H_1$};
  \node[wone, fill=white, inner sep=2pt, font=\small, yshift=-6pt] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.5,T2=0.27,T3=0.23) {$W_1$};
  \node[fill=black!8, inner sep=2pt] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.12,T2=0.46,T3=0.42) {$H_0$};
  \node[wzero, fill=black!8, inner sep=2pt, font=\small] at (barycentric cs:T1=0.22,T2=0.46,T3=0.32) {$W_0$};

  % Vertex labels
  \node[above]       at (T1) {$\theta_1$};
  \node[below left]  at (T2) {$\theta_2$};
  \node[below right] at (T3) {$\theta_3$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The appeal is that the prior lives on the whole simplex, so the non-convex null is no obstacle to writing the test down.
:::

## But Type I error control matters

- $B_t$ is a martingale under the prior mixture $P_{W_0}$, not under each $P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$, $\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta_0$.
- So "reject when $B_t > 1/\alpha$" is not risk-limiting in general.
- A likelihood ratio test does not just work either. **More on that later.**

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
Say the last line exactly as written. It is repeated verbatim when the loop closes in the higher-dimensions section.
:::

# Bayesian audits (last year)

## Controlling Type I error with a maximum sample size

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Fix a maximum sample size $T$. Then $\bar B = \sup_{t \le T} B_t$ is bounded.
- Threshold: the worst-case $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $\bar B$ over $\Theta_0$.
- Symmetric Dirichlet priors: the worst case is on the boundary, and Monte Carlo puts it at the two-way tie.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fetch}
slides/fig/worst_case_cdfs.svg, from figures/worst_case_cdfs.pdf (recipe A).
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The worst case being the two-way tie will come back: in the K = 2 likelihood ratio the tie is the whole story.
:::

# E-variables and martingales

<!-- Section budget: 6 minutes, 7 slides, including widget 1. -->

## E-variables: bets against the null

- An *e-variable* is $E \ge 0$ with $\mathbb{E}_P[E] \le 1$ for every $P$ in the null [@vovk2021evalues; @RamdasGameTheoretic2023].
- Reject when $E \ge 1/\alpha$. By Markov's inequality this is level $\alpha$.
- Betting reading [@Shafer2021]: $E$ is the payoff of a bet that costs 1. The house accepts only bets that cannot win on average under the null.
- Evidence is money won.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The gambler believes Q, the house believes the null. Keep this picture; log-optimality is the gambler's strategy.
:::

## Optional stopping and optional continuation

- A *test supermartingale* $S_t$: $S_0 = 1$, nonnegative, a supermartingale under every null distribution.
- Ville's inequality [@ville]: $P(\sup_t S_t \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha$.
- So stop whenever you like, and stopped $S_\tau$ is still an e-variable.
- Continue whenever you like: reinvest the winnings, and products of e-variables from successive batches stay valid.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
Optional continuation is what the batch construction at the end relies on, so say it here.
:::

## Two candidates: the likelihood ratio

$$E = \prod_{t=1}^n \left(\frac{\mu}{\nu}\right)^{X_t}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{1-\nu}\right)^{1-X_t},
\qquad
g(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[E] = \left(\theta\frac{\mu}{\nu} + (1-\theta)\frac{1-\mu}{1-\nu}\right)^n.$$

<!-- Fallback PNGs still to capture with the snapshot button: the four demo states in the notes. -->

```{=html}
<div id="gw1"></div>
<script>GW.line({ fig: "gw1", mu: 0.6, nu: 0.5, n: 10, name: "widget1" });</script>
```

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes, including the demo.
The curve always crosses 1 at theta = nu. That is the fact that fails in two dimensions.

Demo: drag the blue triangle (mu) and the vermillion circle (nu) along the axis. nu snaps to 1/2.

1. Start at nu = 1/2: the curve crosses 1 exactly at the tie, valid.
2. Drag nu to 0.4: the curve crosses 1 at 0.4, and the band (0.4, 0.5] goes above 1 (thick stroke).
3. Drag nu to 0.55: valid again, but the growth readout drops.
4. Move the n slider: the curve steepens but still crosses 1 at nu.
   This is monotone likelihood ratio at work, and why one null point serves every n.
:::

## Log-optimality

- Many e-variables are valid. Which is best?
- Growth $\mathbb{E}_Q[\log E]$: a gambler stopping at $1/\alpha$ needs about $\log(1/\alpha) / \mathbb{E}_Q[\log E]$ rounds [@Breiman1961; @Kelly1956].
- For a point alternative $\mu > 1/2$, the likelihood ratio against the tie is log-optimal.
- For a mixture $Q = P_{W_1}$ over the alternative, $p_{W_1}/p_{1/2}$ is log-optimal for $Q$.
- The tie is already a mixture over the null. It just has one atom.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The last bullet is the setup for the resolution later: in higher dimensions the optimal denominator is a genuine mixture.
It also explains last year's result: the worst case of the Bayesian audit was the two-way tie for the same reason.
:::

## Martingales with an estimator

- Replace the fixed $\mu$ by a predictable estimate $\hat\mu_t$ from $X_1,\dots,X_{t-1}$:
$$S_t = S_{t-1}\left(\frac{\hat\mu_t}{1/2}X_t + \frac{1-\hat\mu_t}{1/2}(1-X_t)\right).$$
- Still a test supermartingale for $\theta \le 1/2$, whatever the estimates.
- This is ALPHA [@alpha_mart], the method used in practice.

::: notes
Timing: 45 seconds.
No need to specify ALPHA's truncated shrinkage estimator.
:::

- One ALPHA martingale $S^{(j)}_t$ per pair, ignoring ballots for neither candidate.
- Certify once every pair has crossed $1/\alpha$.

::: notes
Timing: 45 seconds.
The figure shows each pair as a projection to a one-dimensional problem with the tie as its null point.
:::

## It is a minimum

- Certifying when every pair has rejected means thresholding $\min_j E_j$.
- $\min_j E_j$ is an e-variable for $\Theta_0 = \bigcup_j \Theta_{0j}$: under $\Theta_{0j}$ it is at most $E_j$.
- The log-optimal e-variable is a likelihood ratio $dQ/dP^*$.
- **Surely the optimum does not contain a min?**

::: notes
Timing: 45 seconds.
Leave it as a question. The answer we can give at a fixed sample size is on the conjecture slide at the end.
:::

## So work in the original dimension

- Build one e-variable for $\Theta_0$ directly, in $K - 1$ dimensions.
- Then compare it with the minimum of the pairwise ones.

::: notes
Timing: 20 seconds. A transition slide.
:::

## A likelihood ratio does not just work

:::: {.columns}


- *More on that later:* this is later.
- One null point $\boldsymbol\nu$ against the alternative $\boldsymbol\mu$:
$$g_{\boldsymbol\nu}(\boldsymbol\theta) = \left(\sum_i \theta_i \frac{\mu_i}{\nu_i}\right)^n.$$
- $g = 1$ is a straight line through $\boldsymbol\nu$. A non-convex null is never on one side of it.

Demo: drag nu (vermillion) along the boundary theta1 = theta2 from the centre to the edge, then try the other piece.
The dashed g = 1 contour stays a straight line through nu, and part of the hatched null is always red (above 1): the max over the null never drops below 1.
Then raise n: the region above 1 gets more extreme but the line does not move.

## The resolution: mixtures over the null

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Denominator $p_W = \int p_{\boldsymbol\theta}\, dW(\boldsymbol\theta)$ for a mixing measure $W$ on $\Theta_0$.
- The *reverse information projection* $P^*$ minimises $\mathrm{KL}(Q \,\|\, P_W)$ over such mixtures [@safetesting; @Lardy2024Reverse].
- $E^* = dQ/dP^*$ is the log-optimal e-variable [@safetesting; @Larsson2025NumeraireRipr].
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

Controls: click in the null to add an atom (weight 2/(k+2), the Frank-Wolfe open-loop step size; say so).
Scroll over an atom to change its weight, drag to move it, double-click to remove it.
"Frank-Wolfe step" adds an atom where g_W is largest over the null: the oracle.
"Reweight" is one EM weight update with the atoms fixed; it cannot increase KL.

## How do you find the RIPr?

- Minimising $\mathrm{KL}(Q \,\|\, P_W)$ over $W$ is fitting a mixture model to $Q$, with atoms constrained to $\Theta_0$.
- Convex in the weights, not in the atoms. The null is not convex either.
- Three algorithms:
  - Frank–Wolfe [@FrankWolfe1956; @Jaggi2013; @TuynmanMathieu2026] and Li–Barron [@LiBarron1999]: add one atom at a time.
  - Expectation–maximisation: move and reweight a fixed set of atoms. TODO: add Dempster, Laird and Rubin (1977) to bibliography.bib from the manuscript.
  - A hybrid: Frank–Wolfe steps interleaved with EM sweeps.

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute.
The oracle, which picks where the next atom goes, is a global non-convex search. That is where the difficulty lives.
:::

## The fitting algorithms at work

```{=html}
<div id="gw6"></div>
<script>
(function () {
  var T = (window.GW_DATA || {}).traces;
  if (!T) { document.getElementById("gw6").textContent = "Trace data missing: run slides/data/make_traces.R, then slides/data/bundle.py."; return; }
  GW.playback({
    fig: "gw6",
    scenarios: [
      { label: "default start", runs: [
        { title: "EM", trace: T.EM }, { title: "Frank–Wolfe", trace: T.FW }, { title: "Hybrid", trace: T.hybrid }] }
    ]
  });
})();
</script>
```

<!-- Fallback still to record: an MP4 or GIF of the playback. -->

::: notes
Timing: 2 minutes.
Frank-Wolfe attacks the bound directly but converges slowly. EM is fast but cannot add atoms. The hybrid takes both.

Traces are real ripr runs (slides/data/make_traces.R): n = 10, mu = (0.45, 0.35, 0.20), 2 s of step time per method.
Time is ripr's step clock, excluding the gap sweeps. Speed is a multiple of real time: at the default 0.1x the 2 s runs play in 20 s.
Wall-clock sync is the honest comparison and matches the manuscript's figures; iteration sync is easier to follow.
The diamonds are the certified growth KL - log U at the end of each run.

Default start: ripr's default init already puts one atom in each piece, so EM does very well here.
:::

## Close is not enough

- If $g_W > 1$ anywhere in the null, $dQ/dP_W$ is **not an e-variable at all**.
- An approximate projection, however close, gives an unfair bet [@safetesting].
- Fix: divide by the worst case, $G_W = \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta_0} g_W(\boldsymbol\theta)$.
$$E_W = \frac{1}{G_W}\frac{dQ}{dP_W} \quad\text{is an e-variable, and}\quad \mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P_W) - \log G_W \le \mathbb{E}_Q[\log E^*] \le \mathrm{KL}(Q\,\|\,P_W).$$

::: notes
Timing: 1 minute. This is the central idea of the manuscript; slow down here.
Careful wording: exceeding 1 somewhere means invalid, not merely suboptimal.
:::

::: notes

Validity is decoupled from the optimiser: any fit, stopped anywhere, gives a real e-variable, and log G_W measures what it cost.

The colour now shows g_W / C and the dashed contour sits at g_W = C. The "max r(c)" tick is the trivial end:
dividing by it always gives a valid e-variable that never exceeds 1, valid and useless.

Demo: with one atom, drag C up (or press "C = grid max") until the contour clears the null, and read off the growth cost.
Then add the second atom: the C needed drops towards 1, and the interval narrows.
:::

## Bounding the worst case

- A search over $\Theta_0$ only finds points, so it can only under-report $G_W$.
- An upper bound must cover every point: branch and bound over the null.
- For multinomials, $g_W$ is already a Bernstein polynomial whose coefficients are the ratios $r(\boldsymbol c)$. TODO: cite Garloff (1985) and Leroy (2012); add both to bibliography.bib from the manuscript.
- Implemented in the R package ripr.

# The ALE manuscript

<!-- Section budget: 3 minutes, 3 slides. -->

## ALE: testing under the influence with approximately log-optimal e-variables

With David and Damjan. arXiv target: November 2026.

1. A recipe that turns any approximate projection into an e-variable, with its growth bracketed.
2. A comparison of Li–Barron, Frank–Wolfe, EM and a new hybrid, on growth against wall-clock time.
3. Rigorous branch-and-bound bounds on $G_W$: Bernstein enclosures for multinomials, and a finiteness criterion for Gaussian location nulls.

- Open-source R package ripr.

Timing: 1 minute.

# What this unlocks

## Question 1: how many atoms does the RIPr need?

- For $K = 3$ and a point alternative, two atoms suffice in every case I have run.
- Conjecture: $K - 1$ atoms suffice for a point alternative. Is there an analytic form?
- For mixture alternatives, almost certainly not.

:::

## Question 2: how optimal are the pairwise martingales?

- At a fixed sample size nothing beats $E^*$, so the pairwise minimum is no better.
- $E^*$ is not a martingale, but batches of it multiply into one (optional continuation).
- How does the batch-sequential test compare with ALPHA per pair?
- Conjecture: batches win at moderate $n$, and the gap vanishes as $n \to \infty$, which would make the pairwise approach admissible.

::: notes
Timing: 1.5 minutes.
This is the question the thesis was organised around. It is the main study for November and December.
Expect the question: what happens if an audit has to stop mid-batch?

## Conclusion

- The question: what does decomposing the plurality null into pairs cost?
- Last year: a direct Bayesian test, valid up to a horizon.
- This year: direct e-variables that are log-optimal up to a measured gap, for any fit.
- Next: batch-sequential audits against the pairwise martingales, to answer the question.

## Why sampling with replacement? {visibility="uncounted"}

- A mathematical device, not a physical requirement: reuse ballots already drawn whenever the model asks for a repeat.
- The cost is the finite-population correction, expected to be small for large elections.

::: {.fetch}
slides/fig/alpha_sampling_effort.svg (recipe A).
:::

## Is any Bayes factor an e-process for $K > 2$? {visibility="uncounted"}

- For $K = 2$ the projection is the tie at every $n$, so the Bayes factor is a test martingale.
- For $K > 2$ preliminary calculations show the projection depends on $n$.
- Conjecture: no Bayes factor of this form is an e-process. Not yet proved.

## How does this differ from Tuynman and Mathieu (2026)? {visibility="uncounted"}

- They fit the projection with Frank–Wolfe and stop when iterates stop changing [@TuynmanMathieu2026].
- Their guarantees are for the exact projection.
- Here the final iterate is accepted as suboptimal, and the bound restores validity and measures the gap.
- The Gaussian example goes beyond finitely supported distributions.
